THE CURRENT NEWS.
SOME RECENT TERRIBLE TRAGEDIES.
Wm. C. McCamus, president of the Schenectady City national bank, committed suicide by shooting himself at midnight. Ill health was probably the cause.

Edward Isom, a clerk in a store at Kerr Station, fourteen miles from Little Rock, Ark., was murdered and robbed by an unknown assassin.

Gus Miller and Matthew Jones have been arrested at Kansas City, Mo., charged with inciting the mob of 1,000 persons which, on April 30, hanged Levi Harrington, colored.

An avalanche in Little Cottonwood, Utah, recently swept over the Richmond and Teresa mine, burying beyond reach to help Robert Greaves, the lessee of the mine.

The Pullman palace car shed and shop at New Orleans, together with three coaches and a large quantity of bedding and other supplies, burned on Saturday. Loss, $75,000.

Heavy forest fires are raging between Green Bush and the Black river, as far as Alcona, Mich. Unless rain comes speedily there will be great damage done to the pineries.

Daniel Johnson and Alfred Wright, colored laborers in the suburbs of Atlanta Ga., died suddenly returning from cutting outs. The men were overheated, and cooled off suddenly.

The League of American Wheelmen, composed mainly of bicyclists from New England and New York, meet to-day in Chicago. About two hundred delegates will be present.

A series of heavy thunder-storms occurred along the Hudson on Saturday. The Rochdale woolen mills, owned by the estate of Elias Titus, were struck by lightning and entirely destroyed. The loss is estimated at from $40,000 to $50,000; partially insured.

During a fight among bridge-builders at Hardeeville, South Carolina, on Saturday night, a colored man was killed by a white man, it is alleged, in self-defense. The negroes attempted to lynch the killer, but were prevented.

A banquet was given by the Commercial club of Chicago, on Saturday night, in honor of the commercial bodies of Cincinnati and St. Louis. 167 covers were laid, and the capital represented is estimated at $140,000,000. Among the guests were Postmaster General Howe and Lieutenant General Sheridan, and the latter "surprised the company by making an excellent speech of some length."

There is great excitement over Secretary Teller's decision opening the Turtle Mountain district. This region includes 9,000,000 acres of the finest land in Dakota, comparatively well wooded and watered, lying north and west of Devil's Lake. It has been closed hitherto by a claim of a wandering band of Chippewa Indians, now declared invalid. Two railroads, the Northern Pacific and the St. Paul, Minneapolis & Manitoba, will build into the region at once and thousands of settlers are ready to rush in as soon as it is formally opened.

Jesse Williams and Frank Miller, two burglars, entered the residence of H. P. Moore at night. The house was surrounded. Miller, in attempting to shoot down Mr. Henry Blackford, was cut down with a scythe. His head was partially severed, the tendons and arteries being cut through.

Ties were piled on the track between Hartford and Meriden, Conn., on Friday night and the Washington express train south was stopped by a watchman. There is a suspicion that this is another fraudulent trick of employees of the road, but nothing positive is known. The officials are investigating the matter.

In the supreme court of Washington county, R. I., a decree has been entered divorcing Catharine Chase-Sprague from William Sprague, giving Mrs. Sprague the custody of her three daughters and permitting her to resume her maiden name, with leave hereafter to apply for alimony if she chooses.

Willie Haley, of Pownal, Vt., aged 11 years, asked a friend how much poison would kill a boy. He was informed that three tablespoonfuls of Paris green would suffice. He took that amount of the poison and died next morning. His father killed himself a few months by cutting his throat and then hanging himself to a door latch. The boy had curly hair and was a handsome little fellow. He said he didn't want to live any more.

In Denver Phil. Hubbard, a jockey employed by Dick Mackey, a well known western horseman, met C. H. Wood, a real estate agent, and knocked him down and began beating him, when Mackey pulled Hubbard off. Upon arising Wood drew a revolver and began firing at Hubbard, hitting him twice. A stray shot struck John Denny, a Western Union telegraph repairer, passing through his thigh. It is thought by some that Mackey was also shot. He was driven away. Hubbard will probably die.

Committing Suicide With Poison.

In Eric, John Daley died suddenly on Thursday. He was believed to have committed suicide by taking poison. The friends of the family were indignant at the published report and said that Daley died a natural death. It was suspected that the true cause was being concealed to save insurance. The coroner was called and a post mortem held. A quantity of corrosive sublimate was found in the stomach and a verdict was rendered of suicide by poison.

What a Married Daughter Witnessed.

John Smith, an old California ranchman living near Milford, two hundred miles southwest of Salt Lake, quarreled with his wife, and seizing a double barreled shot gun, fired at her twice, both charges taking effect. He then coolly reloaded the weapon, went out of the door, fastened a string to the trigger, and placing the muzzle to his breast, fired six navy bullets into his body. He died two hours afterwards. A married daughter witnessed the tragedy. The old man was subject to fits of lunacy.

A Ball Dog Revolver's Work.

Struck an Iceberg.
St. JOHN's, N. F., May 28.—The steamer Friary, twelve days from Newport, England, bound to New York, with iron and tin, put in here to-day for repairs. About noon Thursday, 800 miles east of Cape Spear, during a dense fog, the vessel struck an iceberg, carrying away bowsprit, figurehead, and smashing in ten or twelve feet of her bows, above the water line. Part of the berg, under water, penetrated the steamer's bottom, causing a large opening forward of the water-tight bulkhead. A diver this afternoon found the port bow stove from No. 9 to 20. No damage aft the bulkhead. The repairs will occupy two weeks. The royal mail steamer Plover arrived from the northward to-day. She encountered large quantities of ice in Green Bay, and had her bows badly damaged.

BROOKLYN, May 28.—Services in memory of Abraham Lincoln were held this afternoon at the monument at the entrance of Prospect Park in the presence of a large concourse of visitors. The monument was decorated with flowers.

PROVIDENCE, May 28.—The trustee of the Sprague estate now advertise the property to be sold in parcels—the print works on the 29th of June and various parcels of real estate in this city on June 27 and July 1.

TELEGRAPHIC TWISTINGS.

—Yellow fever is raging at Havana at a frightful rate.

—Minister Sargent has been received at Berlin by the Crown Prince and Princess.

—The Novoe Vremya of St. Petersburg announces that General Albedinski intends to resign the governorship of Poland.

—Archbishop McCabe was enthroned as Cardinal with imposing ceremonies at the Catholic Cathedral in Dublin, on Sunday.

—Frank H. Stone and Arthur J. Cole, of Chicago, were drowned by the capsizing of their boat in Geneva Lake, Saturday.

—The lumbermen's association of Chicago increased the price of 1½ inch mixed lumber one dollar and timber joists and scantlings fifty cents.

—The Catholic clergy of London are about to commence preaching a crusade among the Irishmen of their flocks against connection with secret societies.

—Crickmore, Vanguard, Thora, Bounce, and Judge Murray were the winners at Pimlico on Saturday. French pools paid $5.00, $6.65, $7.10, $20,55, and 20.85.

—William C. McCamus, president of the Schenectady City National Bank, committed suicide by shooting, at midnight last night. Ill-health was probably the cause.

—George A. Conly, the wonderful basso, and Herman Rietzel, the pianist, of the Kellogg Opera Troupe, were drowned in Lake Spofford, New Hampshire, Saturday, while fishing.

—Bicyclists forming the League of American Wheelmen are now in Chicago to the number of 200, chiefly from New York and New England. They will hold a convention there, beginning to-day.

—Mrs. Susan Willis Fletcher, who was imprisoned in England on a charge of obtaining jewels from Mrs. Davis through alleged spiritualistic influence, reached New York Sunday on the steamer Celtic.

—The steamer San Juan, built for the Pacific Mall Steamship Company, was launched at Roach's yard Saturday. Her dimensions are: Length, 283 feet; beam, 36 feet; depth of hold, 25 feet, and tonnage 2,000.

—Ten Kickapoo Indians, living on a reservation in Atchinson County, Kan., were naturalized by the United States court at Topeka, and are now full American citizens, under the act recently passed by Congress.

—Fellowplay, Pinafore, Brother to Grimstead, Rochester, Bancroft, Bondholder, Hindoo, Lida Stanhope, and Maggie Ayer won at the Louisville races Saturday. Miss Malloy and Suananoa ran a dead heat in the last race—a Steeplechase.

—In an affray at Savannah, Ga., among the hands building the bridge over the Savannah at Hardeeville, S. C., a negro was killed in self-defense by a white man from Baltimore. The negroes attempted to lynch the latter, but were prevented.

—The French authorities in Tunis are greatly irritated by intelligence that Turkish troops have disembarked near the frontier between Tripoll and Tunis, in order to reinforce a camp already existing. The submission of the insurgent Arabs is now regarded improbable.

—P. T. Barnum sailed for Europe Saturday. To a reporter he said: "I'm going over with an eye to business. I intend to hire two and a half steamers from the Monarch line and take over the whole show next October. Bailey put me up to it. 'Bailey,' says I, 'the thing will cost $100,000,' 'What of it?' says Bailey; 'we'll take it in the first ten days.' Jumbo is to go along."

Edward Hanlan, the champion sculler of the world, arrived in New York Saturday from Liverpool on the City of Richmond. He does not like the idea of traveling to Manitoba for the next race, but thinks the inducement offered in the case of the match with Ross—$5,000 besides the stakes—sufficient to justify the trip. His future movements are uncertain. His friends in Toronto are getting up a reception for him, and he will shortly have to go there, but his stay in New York will extend over some days. Before leaving England he declined two offers, one of £1,000 for six months, the other of a like amount yearly for five years, to remain and give exhibitions and lessons in rowing.

ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A1:
SERIOUS ROW AT STRONG CITY.
The Outgrowth of Whisky and an Old Feud, Resulting Fatally to George Babb.
George Babb.

We learn from H. R. Fleetwood, who was one of a large number that went from this city to Cottonwood Falls last evening to attend the dedication of the colored Masonic lodge at that place, that a disgraceful and serious row occurred, in which G. O. Babb, a stone mason, was fatally shot. It seems that there is and has been an ill feeling for a long time between those living in Strong City and the Falls. Last night after the lodge exercises proper were over, the crowd dispersed and went over to Strong City, where a public installation of officers was had, which was followed by a dance in the hall. About eleven o'clock the trouble began, induced, no doubt, by the rather free indulgence in whisky, which fired the passions and renewed thoughts of the existing bad feelings between the two towns. As near as we have been able to get at the facts, one of the Falls boys tried to gain admittance to the dance without paying the requisite dollar. After the passing of a few harsh words with the door keeper, he was slapped in the face by the latter. This was promptly resented, and a general melee occurred, in which five persons received wounds. Word was dispatched for the sheriff, and in response Jabe Johnson hurried in the direction of the row. On his way there he received a shot in the hand, from a party he ordered to halt as he was on his way from the hall. It so happened that a construction train, with a large force of men was at Strong City, and they also mingled in the affray, pulling out for the west as soon as the affair was over. They are being pursued by Deputy Sheriff Johnson and posse of citizens. Early this morning Deputy Sheriff Cramer, of this city, received a telegram from Deputy Sheriff Johnson requesting him to arrest a certain party here, a negro who has been working for W. F. Ewing, under several aliases—Ben Ray being his real name. Cramer sought his man, arrested and placed him in jail to await the course of events. The man arrested here by Cramer acknowledges having been in the row, and narrowly escaped serious injury, a stray ball having passed through his pants leg. A small boy of Strong City received a bullet wound in the neck, but we learn none of the wounded five are badly injured. Excitement runs high at Cottonwood Falls, and it is not at all improbable that much trouble will result from last night's affray. The authorities think it unsafe for Ray to be taken away from this city for fear of mob violence. A large number of warrants have been issued, and several arrests will be made in the vicinity of the Falls.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A2:
DIDN'T FIND THEM IN.
A Gang of Armed Men Gather at the Chase County Jail.
To Avenge the Murder of Babb, but Find the Prisoners Flown.
By special advice from Cottonwood
To Avenge the Murder of Babb, but Find the Prisoners Flown.

By special advices from Cottonwood Falls, we learn that a mob numbering about one hundred and fifty, organized at Strong City Sunday, their purpose being to lynch the colored men, Ed. Bridges, Ben Ray, alias Scraggs, and Geo. Blakeman, who were in confinement at Cottonwood Falls on a charge of being participants in the serious row which lately occurred at Strong City, the particulars of which we have already published.

About ten o'clock at night information was given Sheriff Balch that such a mob had formed and with the above purpose. The sheriff at once set about to frustrate such a movement and with this view he procured a team, and securing the three culprits, set out for the jail at Eureka, Greenwood county. He had not been gone over ten minutes when the mob surrounded the jail, armed to the teeth, and called for the prisoners. Upon learning that they had been out-witted by the sheriff, and the birds had flown, no one knew in what direction, they were obliged to content themselves with loud words of imprecation and the discharging of their revolvers in the air. This, for the time, seemed to satisfy them, but finally becoming disgusted at not finding the prisoners, they dispersed.

Sheriff Balch is likely now in Eureka with his men, where they will be confined until the setting of the Chase county court, which will convene about the middle of May.

We are sorry that the citizens of Strong City should seek to take the law in their own hands, even though they consider the case an aggravated one, and hope that better counsels will prevail with them in future.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A4:
Taken to Cottonwood.
Last Sunday the sheriff of Chase county, in company with Deputy Sheriff Jabe Johnson, arrived in Emporia after the three negro prisoners implicated in the recent shooting affray at Strong City. They left on the 4 o'clock train this morning for Cottonwood, where Bridges and Blakemore will to-day have their preliminary examination. Ray was arraigned some time ago, when he waived examination, and in default of $8,000 bail was committed. The attorneys for the defense, so we learn, will ask for a change of venue, as they claim an im partial trial cannot be had in Chase county. The prisoners will doubtless now be lodged in the jail at Cottonwood, as matters have greatly quieted down, and no fears of mob violence are entertained. The trial of these men will not occur until the sitting of the Chase county district court some time in June.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A5:
THE BARB SHOOTING CASE.
Bridges Convicted of Murder in the Second Degree.
Messrs. Buck and Cunningham came in from Cottonwood Falls Friday, where they have been taking a silt in one of the murder cases there. It will be remembered that on April 4 the colored people at Strong City had a Masonic installation, supper and dance, and that one of the colored men named Alex. Blakeman and a white man named George Babb, being drunk, got into some fuss, and Blakeman slapped Babb in the face, for which Blakeman was at once tried and convicted of assault and battery and is now in jail for inability to pay the costs.

A half hour later in the evening some ten shots were fired on the sidewalk and in the street, and a colored man named Ed. Bridges got shot through the arm and across the breast. Another colored man by the name of Wes. Walker was shot in the hand, and George Babb received two shots, either of which were fatal, and died on the morning of April 8th. The coroners' jury decided that Walker, Bridges and Ray did the shooting of Babb. Walker ran away and the county attorney filed an informatoin against Bridges, Ray and Blakeman. Bridges tried to get a change of venue but failed. The papers at the time mentioned the organization of a mob to take the prisoners out and hang them. The county attorney, sheriff and some others brought the prisoners here and they were kept in our jail till May 8.

A nol. pros. has been entered as to Blakeman. Bridges has been tried and convicted of murder in the second degree. Motion for a new trial in his case is set for the 26th inst.

Six witnesses swore that Bridges fired the first shot and hit Babb, and six witnesses swore that Bridges had no weapon, did not shoot, and that Babb fired the first shot. The jury seems to have given the state the benefit of the doubt.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A8: Chase County Leader: A special session of court was held last Tuesday, with C N. Sterry as judge pro tem. A motion for a new trial in the Bridges-Babb murder case was argued and overruled, and Bridges was sentenced to the penitentiary for ten years, after which court adjourned until Monday.
ed-bridges-cottonwood-falls-1882-04-09.A9:
Acquitted.
heretofore report
We have heretofore reported the litigation growing out of the killing of George Babb, at Strong City, April 4th, 1882. One Wes Walker, being advised that he might be roughly handled if caught, skipped out. Walker had been shot in the hand, Ed. Bridges in the arm and body, and Babb had received two wounds, either of which was mortal.

Bridges was tried in June last and convicted. His attorneys, Buck & Cunningham, have argued his case in the supreme court and expect a new trial. Ray was acquitted. Walker was recently arrested and bound over to court. On Thursday a jury was impaneled. Judge Buck went over to defend, and on Saturday they tried out the case, the jury going out a little before 10 p. m., and in two hours returned a verdict of not guilty. It is claimed that Walker was in a better position to have shot than Bridges, but the testimony at the Bridges trial was so strong on Bridges that there was not enough left to go around; hence the evidence against Walker was slight.

A History of T. C. Early's Crime at Leadville, Colorado, on Tuesday Last.

Shortly before 3 o'clock this afternoon, one of the most terrible tragedies in the history of Leadville took place on upper Harrison avenue, the victim being Officer Samuel Townsend, one of the oldest and most popular officers of Leadville, and his slayer, Thomas C. Early, a leading young lawyer of this place. At the hour mentioned, the passers-by on Harrison avenue, near the corner of Fifth, were startled at the loud report of three pistol shots, one following the other in quick succession, and a thin, blue cloud of smoke, that curled and drifted from the hallway of the Union block, located the spot where one man stood with heated weapon clenched within his hand and another writhed in the agonies of dissolution. The crowd that hurried around the hallway were horror-stricken to see the well-known form of Officer Sam Townsend, the constable of Judge Talbot's court, prone upon the landing. Mr. T. C. Early was standing on the stairs, a few steps above, and paused, irresolute which way to go. His hat lay at his feet, and his clothing was disheveled, as though from a recent struggle. Fortunately among the first who were at the spot was Captain John Byrne, the detective in the city's employ, and taking in the situation at a glance, he placed Early under arrest, and hurried with him into Babcock's hat store next door. 'Ere this time the word that a murder had been committed, passed with lightning-like rapidity from mouth to mouth, and the pavement was blocked by a dense crowd that surged into the street and well nigh trampled one upon the other in their effort to reach the scene of the killing. As Byrne arrested Early, several gentlemen lifted Townsend up and carried him across the street to Dr. Dodge's drug store, where he was laid upon a pallet placed upon the floor, and Drs. Dougan and Gallaway were speedily at his side. He was suffering the greatest agony, and it was only with the greatest difficulty that he could be held down while an examination of his injuries was made. His garments were pulled open, and in the abdomen, about three inches above the right groin, a ghastly wound was revealed. The leaden messenger of destruction had buried itself in his bowels, and it was well nigh certain that death was only a matter of the briefest time. A messenger had been sent at once to his wife, and, with his little boy, she arrived in a few moments. The poor woman was scarcely able to realize the magnitude of the blow that had fallen upon her, and kneeling with streaming and agonized eyes by her husband's side, she pressed his hand convulsively to her breast, while the little one with great bewildered eyes stood holding to her dress. It was a sight that will never leave the memory of those who witnessed it.

The case that the quarrel grew out of was a replevin suit brought by a woman named Mamie Mordell against Carrie Adams, the proprietress of a Third street bagnio. Early represented the woman Mordell, and asked for a change of venue. This was granted, and Early claimed that Townsend had over-charged him in fees—a matter of ten or fifteen cents.

Judge Talbott says: "Townsend never either abused Early or threatened to whip him when in my court."

Irving Houser, the jeweler, took Townsend's gun out of its sheath after the shooting, and when it was prone on the landing. It had not been drawn. An eye-witness of the tragedy, a well-known citizen of Leadville, who is familiar with every shooting event in the bloody history of the camp, declares that the cold-blooded and deliberate determination with which Early shot Townsend has absolutely no parallel. The man took deliberate aim, and fired successively without the least sign of fear or trembling. His face, he says, wore an expression that can only be described as devilish in its murderous determination. The victim is a man about forty years of age, and has been a resident of Leadville for about three years. He was a valuable and trusted member of the police force under Chief E. H. Watson, a position which he continued to fill up to a very recent period, having been reappointed by the present administration. He was also, during L. R. Tucker's regime, a faithful and efficient deputy sheriff, and during all his official career demeaned himself in such a manner as to command the confidence, not only of his superiors, but the respect of all with whom his duties brought him in contact. He has at various times engaged in mining, and a short time ago owned considerable mineral property in New Mexico, as well as in the vicinity of Leadville. By a series of reverses, however, he lost nearly all of his possessions, and at the time the calamity overtook him, to-day was, a comparatively poor man. He has a wife and a child, who were immediately notified of the distressing event, and at once hurried to the place where the unfortunate man was dying. Mr. Thomas Chestnut, of the firm of Newman, Chestnut & Stevens, of Pueblo, brother-in-law of Townsend, was notified by telegraph, and will probably come up on the first train.
T. C. Early, the murderer, is a man of perhaps 27 or 28 years. He is a native of the south, and has been a resident of Leadville for perhaps three years. He is a lawyer, and a member of the firm of Danford & Early. He has never enjoyed a very large or lucrative practice, but has engaged in some outside speculations, notably Denver real estate, from which he realized considerable money. A FORMER SEDALIAN

When the lamp is out, the two rods touch each other. To light the lamp, they are pulled apart; and if you look at the flame through a smoked glass, you will see that the rods do not quite touch. There is a small space between their points, and this is filled with fire. Look at the other parts of the rods, or the copper wires that extend along the streets. They have no light, no heat, no sound. The wires are cold, dark, and silent. If we were to push the rods in the lamp close together the light and heat would disappear, and the curious hissing would stop.

The electricity passes down one wire into the other, through the lamp, in silence and darkness, so long as the rods touch and the path is clear. When the rods in the lamp are pulled apart, there is a space to be got over, an obstruction, like rocks in the bed of the brook. The electricity, like water, struggles to get over the hindrance in its path, and it grows whitchot with anger, and flames and hisses as it leaps across the narrow space between the rods. There is another kind of electric lamp, used in houses; it has a smaller and softer light, steady, white and beautiful. In these lamps, also, we have something like the narrow place in the brook. They are made with slender loops of carbon, inclosed in glass globes. The electricity, flowing silently through a dark wire, enters the lamp, and finds only a narrow thread on which it can travel to reach the home-going wire, and, in its struggle to get past, it heats the tiny thread of carbon to whiteness. Like a live ecal, this slender thread gives us a mild, soft light, as long as the current flows. It seems calm and still, but is enduring the same fury of the electricity that is shown in the larger lamps. This is the main idea on which these lamps are made: A stream of electricity is set flowing from a dynamo-electric machine through a wire until it meets a narrow place or a break in the wire. Then it seeks to get past the obstruction, and there is a grand putting forth of energy, and in this way the electric force, although itself invisible is made known to our eyes by a beautiful light. — [Charles Barnard, in St. Nicholas for May.

Postponement of a criminal trial is a rare thing in this Territory, and is never granted without good cause shown, while expensive and protracted criminal trials, such as we once in a while hear of elsewhere, through the the press, are so far as I know things that never have occurred. Witnesses sometimes have to be brought great distances, and the mileage and per diem we pay is high, so that costs sometimes mount up to a considerable sum, but that is due to the sparse settlement of our immense domain and to our disposition to compensate well those whom we compel to attend our Courts.

By the records of this district it appears, that during the last twelve years—and I cannot go back further because the records are imperfect—there have been thirty persons arrested and indicted for homicide under the Territorial law; of these none that I know of escaped before trial except one temporarily, and only one was discharged without trial. Twenty-nine out of the thirty were tried. The trials of twenty-one came off within eight days after indictment. Two of the twenty-nine trials occupied four days, one three days and none of the rest to exceed two days. Only six continuances for one term were granted and three for two terms; one of the former because the jury disagreed; one because the prisoner was a woman great with child and could not be tried without endangering the life of her child as well as her own; one of the latter because at the first term the prisoner could not get his witnesses and at the second had escaped into British Columbia; and the rest by my predecessors for like adequate reasons no doubt. Out of the twenty-nine trials, nineteen convictions were had, each for some grade of criminal homicide, seven for murder in the first degree. Turning now from our survey of the whole district to inspect the record of the Court, which is held at Seattle for the counties of King and Kitsap, and what do we find the trials lasted for the crimes in the first degree. Only one of the twelve has been acquitted. In case of one, the jury disagreed. All the others have been convicted and sentenced. Six of these convictions were for murder in the first degree, two for murder in the second degree, and two for manslaughter. This is a most astonishing record. Where can its parallel be found? Of all the persons held to answer for homicide in this Court for the sixteen years ending January 1st, 1882, only one escaped—only one out of eleven completed trials has resulted in acquittal! Why, on this showing, to indict a man for homicide in this Court is to convict him almost as sure as he is caught. He has only one chance in eleven to escape. And yet the cry is, that the Courts are inefficient!

LATE NEWS ITEMS.
In the Senate, on the 9th, Mr. Call submitted an amendment to the Pensi- rears resolution providing for needy and disabled survivors of the Indian wars prior to 1845, including the Black Hawk, Creek and Seminole wars.

The editorial sanctum of the National Republican, Washington, D.C., was the scene of a tragedy on the night of the 8th. A. M. Soteldo, a committee clerk and newspaper man who had a grievance, called upon Clarence M. Barton, the managing editor, for redress. Pistols were resorted to, and Soteldo was fatally injured, the editor escaping with two slight wounds.

PITNEY, ex-Custodian of the Treasury Department, has revived interest in the contingent fund investigation by adding to his former testimony. He asked to be recalled, Feb. 9th, and stated that he had been informed that Upton and Lamphere had contradicted his testimony with regard to the employees of the Treasury having done work for Secretary Sherman, for which they were paid out of the contingent fund. He reaffirmed his testimony that they had done such work, and had been paid for it out of that fund, and said he was prepared to prove it, and also to prove that Secretary Sherman and Mrs. Sherman knew that this work was so paid for. Senator Hale sprang to his feet, and with some shout of indignation asked: "How dare you charge that Mrs. Sherman knew this?" Pitney replied: "I have received notes from her asking me to send men to do certain work on different occasions, and I have the notes here now." He then produced certain notes, proved to have been written by Mrs. Sherman, requesting that workmen be sent to the Secretary's residence. Pitney added that he had received notes of the same kind from Secretary Sherman, and also produced them.

Leonard managed to catch hold of the wheel and made his way on deck. JUDGE MILLER, of the United States Supreme Court, has issued a writ of error in the case of Charles F. Kring, sentenced to be hanged in St. Louis on Feb. 24th.

A DISPATCH from Tombstone, Ariz., Feb. 8th, says the Coroner’s jury in the case of Wetzel, found murdered by Indians in Dragoon Mountains, charge the responsibility for that and similar offenses on the inefficiency and imbecility of the United States military authorities of the Territory. It is rumored that three more bodies of victims of the Indians have been found in the Dragoon Mountains.

JAMES Low, colored, of St. Louis, was so roughly treated by three of his own color in a Chicago gambling house the other night it was thought he would die. He was pounded with some blunt instrument which fractured his skull.

The following touching incident was telegraphed from Coalfield, Va., the scene of the recent mine horror, on the 7th: Superintendent Dodds mounted a coal car, and, addressing the walling throng of women and children around him, said: "My poor friends, it grieves me to have to state to you that for the present our search for the bodies of those you knew and loved will have to be abandoned. You know what fire in a coal mine means, and it may take months of watching to subdue it. We will close the pit now." The speaker's voice quivered with emotion. When he finished, a beautiful little girl of 14 years, Annie Crowder, the only daughter of one of the victims, uttered a piercing scream and rushed to the mouth of the pit, crying, "Oh, do not leave my dear papa to burn down there! Let me get in the cage and go down after him. Let me save him." The strong arms of the miners held her back as the fragile thing tried to make her way to the cage, and more than one blackened face was made blacker as the hand went up to wipe away the tears. Men sobbed aloud and turned away to conceal their emotion. The little girl, finding her progress barred, swooned at the mouth of the pit.

Having failed to execute some transportation contracts with the Government, James Callaghan, a prominent citizen of San Antonio, Tex., shot himself dead the other day.

FREIGHT trains on the Chicago, Minneapolis & St. Paul Railway telescoped, forty miles west of Eau Claire, Wis., on the 8th. George Winters, engineer, and a conductor were seriously injured.

GEORGE ROBINSON and Mary Baggan, of Chicago, were engaged to be married. On the 19th, Robinson called upon his sweetheart and sent a bullet into her head. He then placed the revolver behind his left ear and fired again, expiring immediately. The girl only lived a few minutes. Mary had refused to go out with Robinson the night previous.

Three murderers were executed on the 10th—Quirino Galtan, a Mexican, at Brownsville, Texas; Jesse Barber, colored, at Winnsboro, S. C.; Henry H. Hall, Prescott, Arizona. Charley Hing, a Chinaman, was hanged at Winnemucca, Humboldt County, Nev., on the 9th, for the murder of Ah Liek, one of his countrymen.

Eddie Kilberger, aged 12, pleaded guilty to manslaughter in the Common Pleas Court at Lancaster, Ohio, a few days ago, and was sentenced to the State Farm until of age. Young Kilberger stabbed a 12-year-old son of Christian Straacks to the heart one evening last October, during a quarrel about some marbles.

Judge Miller, of the United States Supreme Court, has issued a writ of error in the case of Charles F. Kring, sentenced to be hanged in St. Louis on Feb. 24th.

Five members of the Yeager family, of Fort Wayne, Ind., were recently poisoned by raw ham. It was not thought possible for the children to recover.

Two young men recently entered the works of the Chicago Car-wheel Company and asked some information from Walter Todd, the cashier. Almost instantly they threw red pepper in his eyes, pushed him into a closet, locked the door, and seized $400 in cash.

CLARENCE O. PERRY, a boy of 16, was recently left in charge of a house in Ashland, Mass., during the absence of the family. He set fire to three beds in different parts of the house, but the neighbors smelled smoke and extinguished the flames. The fellow was arrested and committed in $3,000 to await the Grand Jury's action. Perry is a monomaniac on the subject of incendiarism and confesses to at least three attempts.

WILLIAM LEDERE, of Syracuse, N. Y., loved Nellis Tait so passionately that he forced entrance to her residence the other day with the avowed purpose of killing her. The proprietress of the house tried to prevent this, and he shot both. He then went home and killed himself by emptying his revolver into his head. Jealousy.

LAKE RANSOM, an employee of the D. M. Osborne Reaper Company for eighteen years and manager of the Chicago office for the last nine years, was found dead in the suburb of Hinsdale, Feb. 11th, brilt away between his house and the depot. Near him was a revolver with two chambers empty, and there was a pistol wound in the back of the head from which the brains oozed. There were evidences of a struggle, but no traces of the murderer. The clothes and wallet had been rifled of their contents. He leaves a family in moderate circumstances.

PARIS advices say the Marquis de Jacas, a large shareholder in the Union Generale, has committed suicide. He had invested 600,000 francs in shares of the Union Generale. It was he who introduced American vines in the south of France.

ALBERT WEILE, an architect, once a wealthy citizen of Cleveland, O.. recently imprisoned as a vagrant at Kansas City, Mo., hanged himself in his cell.

Two coaches attached to an express train on the Wheeling & Lake Erie Railroad rolled into Huron River, about four miles from Huron, O., the other day. The train was going around a sharp bend on which the lower rail had probably been undermined by the recent high water. Thirteen persons were injured.

Five trackmen were killed in a tunnel on the Potomac Railroad, near the Union depot in Baltimore, Feb. 13, by a locomotive on the Western Maryland Railroad. The men were named David Grier, Timothy Kennedy, Edward Birmingham, James Irwin and Patrick McGoff. They stepped from one track to get out of the way of a passing train and walked directly in front of a locomotive on the opposite track.

Elrier Harman, twenty years of age, became enraged at his uncle, John Harman, nearly eighty years old, and picking up a club began a most brutal assault on him. AN OFFICER'S SHOT
Puts an End to the Existence of a Worthless Negro Convict at Overton Station.
He Tries to Brain Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler With an Ax. But Fails.
Yesterday afternoon Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler boarded a Cheasapeake and Ohio train for Overton station, in search of a negro named Bill Williams, an escaped convict from Eusley's plantation. Williams was arrested over a year ago for the shooting of Monroe Alexander, by Captain O'Haver and Sergeant Kuhnholtz. He was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. He worked on Eusley's plantation for several months, and finally made his escape. Before doing so, he set fire to a storehouse, which was

TOTALLY BURNED.

For six months the police have been looking for him, and information reaching them that Williams was in the neighborhood of Overton, the two officers, as already indicated, set out to catch him. Arriving at Overton Station, which is about six miles from here, they left the train and walked about three miles to the east until they came to the shanty of a negro named Cousins. Here they expected to find their man. Officer Butler approached the cabin and

TAPPED AT THE DOOR.

"Who's there?" came from within.

"A friend," said Officer Butler.

"You can't get in."

"Let me in."

"No, sir; the owner of the house told me to let nobody come in."

The officers held a short and decisive conversation. "Push in the door," said the sergeant. Officer Butler did as directed. The door yielded, and opened as it did so. Officer Butler saw the gleam of an ax in the air, and a blow directed at him cut the rim of his hat. He raised his pistol and

PULLED THE TRIGGER,

but the cartridge snapped and the negro bounded out and began slashing at Sergeant Scott with his murderous weapon. He cut the officer's pants with his ax, but did not hurt him. Seeing that the man was desperate and determined not to be taken, and the lives of both the officers being in danger, the sergeant coolly took aim at the negro and shot him. The criminal ran some twenty yards, and then, in the popular criminal language of the day, "fell with a dull thud." The officers held a rapid consultation. The negro was evidently dead, as they heard the

GURGLE IN his THROAT.

Knowing that it was a colored neighborhood and that the negroes would all be soon aroused, the officers started away as fast as they could, leaving the body. They heard the whole country howling shortly afterward, and they prepared to give the dusky recreants a warm reception if they had appeared. A Convict Shot.
MEMPHIS, January 15.—Jim Titus, alias Bill Williams, colored, a convict who escaped six months ago, was shot and killed this afternoon by Sergeant Scott, of the police force, while resisting arrest. The killing occurred ten miles north of Memphis.
jim-titus-memphis.A3:
LATESTELEGRAMS CONDENSED.
A receiver has been appointed for the World's Mutual Relief Association of Lebanon, Pennsylvania.

Three boys were instantly killed in Brook lyn, the other evening, by the falling of an unoccupied building, in which they were playing.

Hank Pruett, a Lake Erie & Western switchman, just recently married, was killed, at Lafayette, Indiana, last Friday night, while stepping in to pull a pin.

The bridge of the Chicago & Alton Road over Salt river, at Mexico, Missouri, went down with a freight train Saturday morning. Nobody, fortunately, was hurt.

A negro named White pawned an overcoat in St. Louis, Saturday night, and was arrested soon thereafter for stealing the same. He was locked up and the coat identified.

Eph Song, the young man who had a leg run over by a train the other day, just south of Winchester, Illinois, and whose leg was amputated, died Saturday from the effects of it.

Thomas Dolan, a section hand working on the Indianapolis & St. Louis road, just east of Pana, Illinois, was struck by the cars Saturday and seriously injured. He died soon after.

A Mrs. Diggins, whose relatives are among the ultra-fashionable in San Francisco, has just been discovered in criminal intimacy with her husband's friend, named Chase. A divorce, is pending.

General Logerot seized several notables at Stax as hostages for the payment of the war indemnity exacted by France. He threatens severe measures if the money is not forthcoming by the end of January.

Jim Titus, a colored convict; who escaped from Eusley's farm near Memphis, about six weeks ago, was shot and killed by Police Sergeant James Scott, a couple of days since. His whereabouts were discovered, but he refused to surrender to the officers, who thereupon shot him.

Two failures were chronicled on Saturday in Memphis, Tennessee. One of them was E. Lehman, retail clothier, who failed for $10,000, with assets about $5,000, and the other was Joseph Mulcahy, retail grocer, whose liabilities were $7,000; assets not known.

Three suspicious characters were arrested at Pana, Illinois, a few days since with a lot of shoes in their possession. They were detained by Marshal Rosenberry till Saturday, when officers from Madison county went after them, they having obtained the plunder by breaking into a freight car on the Chicago & Alton Road near Alton.

A man who passed under the name of William Wilcox made the acquaintance a few months ago of a girl named Mary Cregel, who was working at the Franklin House in Memphis, and succeeded in enticing her into a mock marriage. Two or three days since the whole thing was discovered, and the girl is almost crazy. Detectives are looking for Wilcox.

About 10 o'clock Saturday morning a young man named High Deman fell from the tower of the Union Depot, at St. Joe, Missouri, which he was covering, to the ground below. He fell fully thirty feet. His skull was fractured, one arm broken, a rib broken and other injuries sustained. He was taken up in an insensible condition and taken to the Lindell Hotel and medical aid summened.

An attempt to spread small-pox through the mails was reported to the postal authorities Saturday. An undated and unsigned letter, postmarked Cincinnati, was received by a farmer at Lynn, an office fifty miles north of Richmond, Indiana, in which two small-pox scales were enclosed. The letter read: "I have sent you the small-pox; go home and die." The letter was immediately burned, and the only clue to the perpetrator was thus destroyed, but the best detectives in the country will be set to work on the case.
Sedalia, Missouri, was a couple of days ago the scene of another tragedy. A number of workmen were engaged in erecting a large center-pole for a stone derrick, to be used in removing stone from railroad cars. The pole is about thirty-five feet long, two feet in diameter, and being green oak was very heavy. The workmen had just got the lower end of it into a deep hole and had the pole standing erect. One of the ropes which held it straight broke in two and let the log fall. It crushed Benjamin Ellis to the earth, and crushed him so bad that he died two hours later. Ellis leaves a wife and five children in destitute circumstances.

A fatal accident occurred Saturday afternoon at 1 o'clock on the Missouri Pacific Railroad, near Rose Hill, the first station west of Kirkwood, Missouri. A stranger, supposed to be a stone mason, had been looking for work on the St. Louis & San Francisco construction, and failing to get suitable employment, determined to return to St. Louis. The train was just passing when he got to Rose Hill. In attempting to get on board one of the cars he fell across the rail. A dozen or fifteen cars passed over him, cutting off both legs close up to the trunk. The sight was a horrible one. One leg was crushed out of all shape. The other was found some sixteen feet distant without a scratch upon it excepting where it had been severed from the man's body. Close by, between the rails, was the trunk. The unknown breathed his last as soon as the train men reached him. He was about 40 years of age, and the only paper found upon his body that might possibly lead to his identification, was a letter addressed to "Dennis O'Conol, Bartoid Valley P. O., St. Louis Co., Mo."

HAMPTON, Franklin County, Iowa, is much exercised over the discovery that the late County Treasurer, S. C. McKenzie, is a defaulter to the amount of $8,509. The Board of Supervisors are investigating the matter.

THOS. MORGAN, of Covington, Ky., while delirious from small-pox, jumped from a second-story window and crushed his skull.

A case of either lynching or very strange suicide has come to light near Churchville, Monroe County, N. Y. The body of a young man was found hanging by a halter from the limb of a tree. The man had evidently been dead but a short time. He was well dressed, and appeared to be about 26 years old.

Some seventy operators have been thrown out of work by the burning of a wool mill at Charlottesville, Va. The Adirondack Springs House, Whitehall, N. Y., burned. W. H. Collins, a fireman, was killed.

One seaman was drowned and two others probably fatally burned while fighting flames on the schooner Eugene, at Charleston, S. C.

THOMAS WATERS and Joseph Newton, of Oskaloosa, Iowa, were overpowered by foul air in a coal mine. The former died; the latter will not recover.

FRANK TAYLOR, of Napoleon, O., a Wabash employee, was run down by a yard engine at Toledo, O., and instantly killed.

TOPLIFF, an old resident of Alamakee County, Iowa, committed suicide by hanging.

A CHILD of J. B. Coles, residing near East Liverpool, O., died from drinking concentrated lye left within reach.

THE mother and daughter of John Nebb, a Newark (N. J.) saloon-keeper, were suffocated by a slight fire.

MAJOR HICKS, under sentence of death in the Covington (Ky.) jail, has small-pox.

A DISPATCH dated Yakima, W. T., 12th, says Toma Hop Towne, an Indian, was executed for the murder of Lorenzo D. Perkins and his wife. The murder was committed at Rattlesnake Creek, Yakima County, during the raid in the summer of 1878. Seven Indians were engaged in the murder. Three have been executed, three have been shot while resisting the Sheriff and endeavoring to escape jail, and one released, having turned State's evidence.

J. VAN ALSTEIN, of Princeton, Minn., resisting arrest, was killed by Policeman Turner, who was obliged to fire three shots, two of which took effect. Alstein was in liquor and attacked the officer with a bay-fork.

THADDEUS BABER and William Ward were hanged in St. Louis, Jan. 13. Moreau, the French-Canadian who killed his wife last September, was executed at Rimouski, Canada, on the same day. His head was nearly severed from his body. Joe Hay, Eidridge Scales and Matilda Carter, were hanged at Wentworth, N. C., for the murder of Nash Carter. All colored.

WM. MASON, Waupa, and Jos. Spain, Portage City, Wis., were both killed by runaway teams.

JOHN HAMER, Bucyrus, O., and Mike Riley, Waterloo, Iowa, were killed while coupling cars. The mangled remains of Sol. Davis, of Catlettsburg, Ky., were found on the track, where he had fallen asleep.

F. FRANK, a German farmer, was crushed to death under a load of wood at East Saginaw, Mich. His wagon was upset.

C. H. Gilbert, a farmer residing near La Grange, Ind., committed suicide by taking morphine. He had been drinking for some time and was under the influence of liquor when the deed was committed. He leaves a wife and two children, and was 40 years of age.

MISCREANTS near New Paris, O., removed a rail for the purpose of wrecking a Dayton & Western express train. The mail and express car was badly damaged. The fireman was seriously injured, but the passengers were unhurt.

BATES GALLAGHER was killed and Thomas Wade seriously injured by being thrown from a Cleveland & Pittsburg train near Steubenville, O. A truck became detached from the car.

THOMAS ALEXANDER, a highly respected citizen of Montgomery County, Ky. living in Stepstone, on the Big Sandy Railroad, was run over and killed by a passenger train. He was about 70 years old.

NEARLY the whole business portion of the village of Orwell, Out., was consumed by fire the other night.

MRS. NINNISS died in a dentist's chair at Grass Valley, Cal., while under the influence of chloroform. Everything was done to resuscitate her, but without avail. The Coroner's Jury in the case rendered a verdict that the woman came to her death from syncope, induced by chloroform, and exonerated Dr. Jones.

JIM TITUS, alias Bill Williams, a colored convict who escaped from Ensley's farm six months ago, was shot and killed by Police Sergeant James Scott, ten miles north of Memphis, Tenn., while resisting arrest.

The death is announced of Caroline Richings-Bernard, prominent in English opera some years ago.

She had forced him to sign a deed to the farm and taken the management of it herself. Then she refused to sustain the relation of wife to him any longer. He entered suit to compel her to give back the farm, but compromised by taking half, she agreeing to allow him to occupy the same room with her thereafter. She kept her agreement a few days and then hit him with a boot-jack for kissing her. This was supplemented by a severe thrashing, by the sons. Recently quarreling was renewed in consequence of the sale of a horse, by Daniel, the second son, and Mr. Smith disappeared. Knowing that the boys had threatened the old man's life, neighbors searched for the body and found it in a well, under nineteen feet of water and a pile of stones. There were two holes in the right temple, part of his clothes were torn off, and there were other marks of a scuffle. Investigation led to the discovery that he had been shot by Dan while sitting beside the kitchen fire, and the elder son helped to drag the body out to the barn lot and throw it in the well, while his wife stood guard and kept the smaller children locked up in a bedroom. They were placed under arrest, and a strong guard was necessary to prevent lynching by an excited throng.

There was the usual Wednesday reception yesterday, though with less than the usual formality, at the residence of the Secretary of State. The parlors being at no time crowded, those who were fortunate enough to be of the number who called enjoyed more personal attention from their distinguished hostesses than is possible to the usual throng on Cabinet-ladies' day.

Miss Folger, daughter of the Secretary of the Treasury, was at home from two till five at 1206 Eighteenth street, and was assisted by Mrs. Crowninshield, and also by Mrs. Judge Andrews, of Syracuse and Albany, the wife of Secretary Folger's successor as chief judge of the Court of Appeals, New York. Mrs. Andrews, a charming and accomplished lady, is an intimate friend of Miss Folger, and for several seasons at Albany the two families have shared the same winter residence. Miss Foot and Miss Gardiner, of New York, are still guests of Miss Folger, and were among the callers yesterday at the house of the Secretary of State. Mrs. Senator Voorhees and Mrs. Senator Sherman were also making these Cabinet calls. It is regarded as a very amiable courtesy on the part of the two leading Cabinet families to continue their Wednesday receptions during Lent, as so many strangers entitled to consideration are still sojourning and arriving in the city, to whom the opportunity of paying their respects is a privilege highly appreciated. Miss Folger, though a lady of fine social endowments and tastes, has denied herself of participation in dinner parties and evening receptions this winter, the better to meet her home obligations, and her friends will be happy to know that she has materially gained in health by residence in this mild climate, notwithstanding the exactions upon the strength of a Cabinet hostess whose Wednesdays are so charming. She has dined as a guest only at the Executive Mansion since her coming to Washington. The Wednesday evenings of Mrs. Hunt and the Thursday evenings of Mrs. Frelinghuysen are pleasures enjoyed during Lent by the circie of invited guests.

The statement that the President had endeavored, but was unable on account of the previous demand, to secure a box at the opera on a certain evening of this week was invented and circulated among ticket-buyers as a clever advertising dodge, and had no foundation in fact. Shot and Killed in Prison.

BALTIMORE, March 1.—This afternoon Robert Taylor, a colored convict in the Maryland penitentiary, was shot and killed by Prison Officer James Byrne. Taylor was employed in the foundry and was told by the foreman to go on another floor and make a casting in place of one he destroyed yesterday. He paid no attention to the foreman, when Byrne repeated the order. Taylor replied that he would not go on the other floor, and made an assault on Byrne, when the latter fired. Taylor grappled with the officer, and Mr. Thorne, the foreman, separated them. Taylor than ran for Thorne, but the latter escaped, and he returned to the assault upon Byrne, who fired two more shots, at the last of which Taylor fell and died within an hour. A jury of inquest rendered a verdict that the killing was in self-defense. Taylor was a powerful man, and at times very hard to manage.

A Murderous Convict Shot Down.
BALTIMORE, March 1.—This afternoon at the Maryland penitentiary Robert Taylor, a colored convict from Somerset county, refused to obey the orders of Mr. James Byrnes, one of the deputy warders, and when the latter demonstrated with him he seized a heavy billet of wood and made a murderous onslaught on Byrnes, who finally when hard pressed fired at his assailant three times, killing him almost instantly. The Attempted Assassination of Queen Victoria.
ARREST OF THE MAN WHO FIRED THE SHOT—ATTEMPTS
A cablegram in yesterday's Star announced the firing upon Queen Victoria last evening. A later dispatch from London gave the following particulars: As the Queen was entering her carriage this evening a man in the station-yard deliberately fired a pistol at her. The man, who was a miserable looking object, was immediately seized by several policemen and taken to the Windsor police station. No one was hurt. The man gave his name as Roderick MacLean. The Queen drove off to the castle immediately after she was fired at. The miscreant was followed to the police station by a large crowd of people. The prisoner was with difficulty rescued from the crowd. The Queen arrived at Windsor at 5:25 p.m. She had been in London since Tuesday, where she gave a drawing-room on Wednesday in honor of the Princess Helena, of Waldeck, who is to marry Prince Leopold. A crowd of people assembled at Buckingham Palace this morning in hopes that the Queen would drive out. The demeanor of the people was as cordial as usual. Newspaper hawkers are now (7:30 p.m.) crying the news on the London streets. It causes much sensation.

"There was a large crowd of spectators awaiting the Queen's arrival at Windsor. The Queen walked across the platform of the railway station to her carriage, which was waiting to take her to the castle. John Brown, her attendant, had already ascended to his seat behind the carriage, when a man standing at the entrance to the station-yard, among a number of spectators, pointed a pistol at the carriage and fired. To judge from the report the pistol was not heavily loaded. The Queen, who was probably not aware of what had happened, was immediately driven to the castle, but before she passed the man had been seized by the superintendent of the borough police, who was standing near by. He was also violently seized by the crowd, and was only rescued from them when three or four policemen came to the superintendent's assistance. The pistol was captured by one of the crowd. The prisoner, Roderick MacLean, who was miserably clad, was taken into High street and thence conveyed to the police station in a cab. As soon as the Queen arrived at the castle she ordered an equerry to proceed to the depot to enquire if any one had been hurt. The report of the pistol was sharp, but not loud. MacLean apparently intended firing again, when the revolver, which seemed to be a new one, was knocked from his hand by a bystander and handed to the police. Eton scholars were prominent in the attempt to lynch MacLean. The Right Hon. Sir Henry F. Ponsonby, the Queen's secretary, proceeded to the police station, and after obtaining all the information possible, telegraphed to Mr. Gladstone the facts of the assault. It is understood the Queen has not sustained any shock. MacLean is said to be an inhabitant of the South Sea and is twenty-seven years old. He states that he is a grocer's assistant. The doctors pronounce him sane. The revolver is a six-chambered Colt's, American make. Two chambers were found loaded, and two had recently been discharged. Fourteen ball-cartridges were found on the prisoner. MacLean says that hunger actuated the crime."

Robert Taylor (colored), a convict in the Maryland penitentiary, was shot and killed about 2 o'clock Wednesday afternoon in the foundry at the penitentiary by James Byrne, an officer of the institution. It appears that Taylor, the deceased, had imperfectly done some work the day previous, for which he had been reported by the foreman of the foundry, George W. Thorn, to Officer Byrne, who, under the regulations, sent Taylor to the office of Warden Wilkinson, where he (Taylor) was reprimanded, and told by the warden that he should do the work over after he had finished his task the following day (Wednesday). Accordingly, Wednesday about 1:45 P. M., Mr. Thorn, foreman of the foundry, ordered Taylor, as he had finished his task for the day, to make over the work which he had spoiled the day before. Taylor did not move, and deigned no reply to repeated orders to do the work. Thorn then reported the matter to Officer Byrne, who was in the foundry. That officer ordered Taylor to do the work as instructed by the foreman. Taylor still remained silent, and made no move to obey. Officer Byrne then told Taylor to "go into the office." Taylor said something about getting into trouble, and presently seized a molder's rammer and struck at the officer, who, simultaneously with the demonstration made by Taylor, drew his pistol. As the rammer (a hickory rod one and one-quarter inches in diameter, four feet long, with heavy iron mountings on both ends) descended, the officer threw up his right arm, pistol in hand, received the blow, discharging his pistol, which fell from his hand. The foreman (Thorn) ran up and seized Taylor from behind for a moment or two. Taylor freed himself from Thorn, whereupon Thorn retreated a few steps. Two other shots were fired by Officer Byrne, whose pistol had been returned to him by a convict who was present. Taylor, the colored convict, fell mortally wounded.

INGUAN CRUELTY.
The Brutal Treatment Inflicted Upon a Little Girl in an Illinois Town.

STERLING, Ill., Jan. 31. — It has been discovered that a man and woman named Seymour have been horribly maltreating a fatherless girl, seven years old, whom they were supposed to be taking care of. The child is small for its age, and Seymour compelled her to feed and take care of a horse and bring coal. He confined her in a cellar at times all day without food or clothing, except a thin dress, and punished her with a horsewhip until the surface of her entire body was black and blue and sore. Sometimes he would toss her to the ceiling and let her fall on the floor. No species of cruelty seemed too severe to adopt toward the child. The villagers last night made a determined though unsuccessful attempt to lynch Seymour, but both he and his wife have fled.

The village of Rock Falls, Whiteside county, Ill., was in a ferment on Monday. There lives in the place a Mrs Bolton, whose husband has been sent to the insane asylum, leaving her burdened with eight small children. A Times special thus tells the story:

About a month ago one of the children, a girl 7 years old, went to live with a man and woman named Seymour, and Saturday word reached the mother that her child was being abused. She went to Seymour's to inquire into the matter, and found the child in a horrible state from beating and starvation. The child was taken away, put under a physician's care, and warrants issued for the arrest of the guilty parties. Yesterday a great number of people visited the child, and the examination so maddened them that last night about 10 o'clock from twenty to thirty disguised men went to Seymour's house to lynch him. Word came to the man and his wife and they fled. The residence was searched and a number of other houses examined, but he was not caught. Returned Califormans said it looked like old times, and meant business. The child is small for its age, and Seymour compelled her to feed and take care of a horse and bring in coal. He confined her in the cellar at times all day without food or clothing except a thin dress, punished her with a horse-whip until the surface of the entire body was black and blue and sore, and would toss her toward the ceiling and let her fall on the floor. He prevented her going out doors more than once a day, and then when her clothes were soiled compelled her to clean them with her tongue. He insisted upon the child standing on one foot and then when the would become exhausted whipped her with a horsewhip. No species of cruelty seemed too severe to adopt toward the child. The people of the village are determined to have the fellow puished, and will leave no means tried that will reach that result.
